subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Have you ever wondered what makes a car move, what makes a light bulb glow, or what gives you the strength to run and play? The answer to all of these questions is one amazing word: energy. Energy is everywhere around you, all the time. When you wake up in the morning and the sun rises over Mogadishu, that is energy. When your mother cooks bariis (rice) over a charcoal fire, that is energy. When you kick a football across the sand, that is energy too. In this unit, you will discover what energy really is, the many different forms it takes, and how it moves from place to place to make things happen.

outcomes: Explain what energy is and why it is needed for anything to happen.
Name and describe the main forms of energy: light, heat, sound, movement (kinetic), stored (potential), and electrical energy.
Identify different energy sources, such as the Sun, food, wind, moving water, charcoal, and fuel.
Describe how energy is transferred from one object to another and how it changes from one form to another.
State the big rule of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed or moved.
Explain the difference between renewable energy (like solar and wind) and non-renewable energy (like oil and charcoal).
Give practical examples of how to save energy in your own home and community.
Investigate energy questions fairly and record what you observe.
Before we begin, let us meet the important words of this unit. Do not try to memorise them all at once. You will meet each of them again and again, and soon they will feel like old friends.
The ability to do work or cause a change.

concepts.title: What Exactly Is Energy?
concepts.explanation:
Let us start with the biggest question of all: what is energy? Scientists have a short answer. Energy is the ability to do work or to make something change. That sounds simple, but let us think carefully about what it means. When something has energy, it can push, pull, lift, heat, light up, or make a sound. Without energy, nothing at all would happen. The whole world would be frozen and still, like a photograph that never moves.

Here is a helpful way to think about it. Imagine your friend Amina wants to carry a bucket of water from the well back to her home. To lift and carry that heavy bucket, she needs energy in her muscles. Where did that energy come from? It came from the food she ate that morning, perhaps some canjeero with honey and a cup of sweet tea. Her body took the energy that was stored inside the food and changed it into the energy of movement. This is a perfect example of how energy can move from one place to another and change from one form to another.

One of the most important things to understand is that you cannot usually see energy itself. You cannot hold a handful of energy the way you can hold a handful of sand. Instead, you see what energy does. When you see a boat moving across the water, you are seeing kinetic energy at work. When you feel the warmth of the sun on your skin, you are feeling thermal energy. When you hear the call to prayer travel across the town, you are hearing sound energy. Energy is a little bit like the wind: you cannot see the wind itself, but you can see the palm leaves shaking and feel it on your face, so you know it is there.

[*] Did You Know? The word energy comes from an old Greek word, energeia, which means being active or at work. Every single second, the Sun sends more energy to the Earth than all the people in the world could use in a whole year!

Scientists measure energy in units called joules. You do not need to do difficult sums with joules in Year 4, but it is good to know the word. A tiny amount of energy, like lifting a small pebble, is only a few joules. A huge amount of energy, like the energy in the waves crashing on the beach at Kismaayo, would be millions and millions of joules. The bigger the change something can make, the more energy it has.
concepts.example: Let us think about this some more. Everything that happens in your day is really a story about energy. When the wind rustles the acacia trees, energy is at work. When a donkey pulls a cart of water through the market in Hargeisa, energy is at work. When your heart beats inside your chest, even while you sleep, energy is quietly at work. Because energy is behind absolutely everything, learning to notice it is like being given a special pair of glasses that helps you see how the whole world really works. Once you start looking, you will find energy hiding in every corner of your life.

concepts.title: The Many Forms of Energy
concepts.explanation:
Energy is like water: it can take many different shapes. Just as water can be a solid block of ice, a flowing liquid, or invisible steam, energy comes in many different forms. Let us meet each one, because being able to name the forms of energy is one of the most useful skills a young scientist can learn.

Light energy is the form of energy that lets you see the world. It travels in straight lines and moves incredibly fast, faster than anything else in the universe. Our greatest source of light energy is the Sun. Every morning, sunlight pours down over the savanna, the coast, and the towns, giving light to everyone. Other sources of light energy include a torch, a lamp, a candle flame, and even the screen of a phone. Light energy is so fast that when you switch on a torch in a dark room, the whole room lights up in less than the blink of an eye.

Heat energy, which scientists call thermal energy, is the form of energy that makes things warm or hot. You feel heat energy from the sun on a hot afternoon in Garissa. You feel it from the glowing charcoal when your family cooks goat meat or boils water for tea. Heat energy always moves from hotter things to cooler things. That is why a hot cup of shaah (tea) slowly becomes cold if you leave it: the heat energy escapes into the cooler air around it. It is also why boiling water is such an important way to make well water safe to drink, because the heat energy kills tiny germs.

Sound energy is the energy of vibrations that we hear with our ears. When something vibrates, which means it shakes back and forth very fast, it pushes on the air around it and makes the air vibrate too. These vibrations travel through the air until they reach your ear, and your brain turns them into the sounds you know. When Hassan beats a drum, the drum skin vibrates and makes sound energy. When the muezzin calls the adhan, sound energy travels across the whole neighbourhood. Sound energy needs something to travel through, usually air, which is why there is no sound in empty space.

Any object that is moving has kinetic energy. The word kinetic simply means moving. A galloping camel, a spinning top, a football flying towards the goal, a river flowing to the sea, and the wind blowing along the Indian Ocean coast all have kinetic energy. Here is an important rule to remember: the faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has. A slow-walking donkey has a little kinetic energy, but a fast-running lion has much more. Also, heavier things carry more kinetic energy than lighter things moving at the same speed. This is why a big truck is much harder to stop than a small bicycle.

Potential energy is stored energy that is waiting to be used. It is like energy that is sleeping, ready to wake up. There are a few kinds of stored energy. When you stretch a rubber band or bend a springy stick, you store elastic potential energy inside it. When you let go, that stored energy turns into movement. When a mango hangs high up in a tree, it has gravitational potential energy because of its height. If the stalk breaks, that stored energy turns into movement as the mango falls to the ground. And the food you eat holds chemical potential energy, which your body unlocks to keep you alive and active.

Electrical energy is the energy that flows through wires to power the machines and devices we use. It lights up bulbs, charges phones, and runs fans and radios. In your science learning, you will use safe, low-voltage batteries to explore electrical energy. A battery stores energy and can push it around a complete circuit to light a small bulb. Electrical energy is very useful because it is easy to send along wires from one place to another, and it can easily be changed into light, heat, sound, or movement.
concepts.example: Safety First: For learning about electricity, only ever use small batteries such as AA or AAA. Never, ever use the electricity from wall sockets in your home. Household electricity is very powerful and extremely dangerous. Always keep water away from batteries and electrical things, and ask an adult for help.

concepts.title: Where Does Energy Come From? Energy Sources
concepts.explanation:
Every bit of energy you use comes from somewhere. The place that energy comes from is called an energy source. Let us explore the most important energy sources, especially the ones that matter here in East Africa.

The greatest energy source of all is the Sun. This may surprise you, but almost all the energy on Earth begins with the Sun. Sunlight gives us light and warmth directly. But the Sun also helps plants grow, and plants store the Sun's energy inside them. When a goat eats grass, it takes in that stored energy. When you drink camel milk or eat goat meat, you take in the energy that started as sunlight. Even the wind is caused by the Sun heating the air unevenly. So the Sun is the great giver of energy to almost everything.

Food is the energy source for all living things, including you. Foods like bariis (rice), dates, canjeero, camel milk, bananas, and beans all contain chemical potential energy. Your body is like a wonderful machine that unlocks this stored energy and uses it to keep your heart beating, your lungs breathing, and your muscles working. This is why you feel weak and tired when you are hungry: your body is running low on energy. It is also why a good breakfast gives you the energy to learn and play all morning.

[*] Did You Know? Dates are one of the best natural energy foods in the world. That is one reason many people break their fast in Ramadan by eating dates, because they give quick energy after a long day. A single handful of dates gives your body a fast burst of natural sugar energy.
concepts.example: Other important energy sources include the wind, which carries kinetic energy and is especially strong along the coast and in open savanna. Moving water, such as a flowing river or a waterfall, also carries a great deal of kinetic energy. Charcoal and firewood are energy sources that many families use for cooking; when they burn, they release heat energy that was stored inside the wood. And fuels such as petrol and diesel store a lot of chemical energy, which is why they are used to power cars, buses, and boats.

concepts.title: Energy on the Move: Transfers and Changes
concepts.explanation:
One of the most exciting things about energy is that it never stays still. Energy is always on the move, jumping from one object to another and changing from one form to another. When energy moves from one object to another, we call it an energy transfer. When energy changes from one form into a different form, we call it an energy transformation. These two ideas are at the very heart of understanding energy.

Let us follow the energy on a real journey. Think about your friend Yusuf kicking a football on the sand. First, Yusuf's body has chemical energy from the food he ate. When he runs and kicks, that chemical energy transforms into kinetic energy, the energy of movement. His moving foot transfers energy to the ball, and now the ball flies through the air with kinetic energy of its own. When the ball hits the ground and rolls to a stop, its kinetic energy is transferred to the sand and the air as a tiny bit of heat and sound. The energy did not disappear. It simply moved and changed into other forms.

Here is another wonderful example that shows energy changing back and forth. Imagine a swing in a playground, or a pendulum, which is just a weight hanging on a string. When you pull the swing back and hold it high, it has stored potential energy because of its height. When you let go, the swing rushes down, and that potential energy changes into kinetic energy, so the swing moves fastest at the very bottom. As it rises up the other side, the kinetic energy changes back into potential energy, and the swing slows down. The energy keeps trading between potential and kinetic, over and over, like two friends passing a ball back and forth.
concepts.example: Energy often goes through a whole chain of changes. Think about a solar panel on the rooftop of a house in Hargeisa. Light energy from the Sun hits the panel. The panel changes that light energy into electrical energy. The electrical energy travels along wires into the house. There, it might change into light energy in a bulb, sound energy in a radio, or movement energy in a spinning fan. So the Sun's light becomes electricity, and the electricity becomes light, sound, and movement. What a journey! Following energy through a chain like this helps you understand how the world works.

concepts.title: The Great Rule: Energy Cannot Be Created or Destroyed
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to one of the most important rules in all of science. It is called the conservation of energy, and it says something amazing: energy cannot be created out of nothing, and it cannot be destroyed. It can only be changed from one form to another, or moved from one object to another. This rule is always true, everywhere in the universe, with no exceptions.

This can be a little confusing at first. You might ask: if energy is never destroyed, why does a swing eventually stop? Why does a rolling ball come to rest? Why does a hot cup of tea grow cold? The answer is that the energy did not disappear. It only spread out into other places where we cannot easily see it. When a ball rolls to a stop, its kinetic energy turns into a tiny bit of heat and sound as it rubs against the ground. That heat spreads into the ground and the air. The energy is still there, just scattered too thinly for us to notice.

The rubbing that slows things down is caused by a force called friction. Friction turns useful movement energy into heat energy that spreads away. This is why no machine can keep moving forever on its own. Some people long ago dreamed of building a magic machine that would run forever and give out more energy than it used. We now know this is impossible, because energy can never be created from nothing. A machine can only ever pass along the energy it is given, and some of that energy always leaks away as heat.
concepts.example: [*] Did You Know? The energy in the sunlight falling on East Africa is enormous. Many parts of the region get strong, bright sunshine almost every day of the year, which makes it one of the best places on Earth to collect solar energy.

concepts.title: Renewable Energy and Saving Energy
concepts.explanation:
Some energy sources will run out one day, and some will not. This is a very important difference. Non-renewable energy sources, such as oil, coal, and natural gas, took millions of years to form deep inside the Earth. Once we use them up, they are gone forever, and they can also make the air dirty when they burn. Renewable energy sources, on the other hand, will not run out. The Sun will keep shining for billions of years, the wind will keep blowing, and rivers will keep flowing. This makes renewable energy very special.

East Africa is one of the sunniest places in the world, so solar energy is a wonderful gift here. More and more families are putting solar panels on their rooftops. These panels quietly change sunlight into electricity all day long, with no smoke and no noise. That electricity can light homes at night, charge phones, and run small machines, even in villages far from any power station. A small solar lamp can help a child like Khadija read and study after the sun goes down.

Wind energy is another clean, renewable source. Along the coast near Berbera and Mombasa, and across the open plains, the wind blows strongly. Tall machines called wind turbines have huge blades that the wind pushes around. As the blades spin, they turn the wind's kinetic energy into electrical energy. Moving water can be used in the same way, using the kinetic energy of a river to make electricity.

There is one more clever idea about renewable energy that is worth understanding. Both solar panels and wind turbines take one form of energy and turn it into electrical energy, which is one of the most useful forms because it travels so easily along wires. A solar panel turns light into electricity, and a wind turbine turns movement into electricity. Once we have that electricity, we can use it in hundreds of ways, from lighting a classroom to pumping clean water up from a deep well for a whole village. This is why renewable energy gives so much hope for the future of communities across East Africa and beyond.

Because energy is so precious, we should never waste it. Saving energy protects our world and saves money too. In Islam, taking good care of the Earth is part of being a good khalifah, or caretaker, of Allah's creation, and avoiding waste is something our faith teaches us to value. Here are simple ways you can help save energy every single day:

Switch off lights, fans, and radios when you leave a room or do not need them.

Cook wisely by using a lid on the pot, which keeps heat in and cooks food faster with less charcoal or fuel.

Use daylight for reading and playing instead of switching on lamps during the day.

Unplug chargers and devices once they are full, because they can keep using energy.

Walk or cycle for short journeys instead of using a vehicle, which also keeps you healthy.
concepts.example: Care for solar lamps and batteries so they last a long time and are not wasted.

methods.title: The Swinging Pendulum (Kinetic and Potential Energy)
methods.example: To watch how energy changes back and forth between stored (potential) energy and moving (kinetic) energy.
steps: Tie the heavy object firmly to one end of the string.
Tie or hold the other end of the string to a fixed point so the object can swing freely.
Pull the object gently to one side so it is raised up, and hold it still. Notice that it is now higher up.
Let go (do not push) and watch the object swing back and forth.
Watch closely: at which point does it move fastest? At which points does it pause?

methods.title: The Sunshine Water Warmer (Light and Heat Energy)
methods.example: To show that light energy from the Sun can be changed into heat energy, and that dark colours soak up more heat than light colours.
steps: Fill both cups with the same amount of water at the same temperature.
Wrap one cup in dark cloth and the other in white cloth.
If you have a thermometer, measure and write down the starting temperature of each cup.
Place both cups side by side in a sunny spot.
Wait for about one hour. Try to keep everything else the same, so it is a fair test.

methods.title: The Rubber Band Launcher (Elastic Potential Energy)
methods.example: To show that a stretched rubber band stores energy, and that stretching it more stores more energy.
steps: Hook the rubber band over your thumb, and place the paper ball in the band like a little sling.
Pull the band back only a small amount (for example, 5 cm) and let go, aiming at the open floor, never at anyone.
Measure how far the paper ball travelled and write it down.
Now pull the band back further (for example, 10 cm) and launch again. Measure the distance.
Try a third, even bigger stretch. Measure again.

methods.title: The Pinwheel and the Wind (Kinetic Energy of Air)
methods.example: To show that moving air (wind) carries kinetic energy that can do work by turning a pinwheel.
steps: Fold the paper square corner to corner both ways to find the centre, then unfold it.
Carefully cut along each fold from the corner towards the centre, but stop before you reach the middle.
Bring every other corner into the centre to form the pinwheel shape, and pin them at the middle.
Pin the pinwheel loosely onto the handle so it can spin freely.
Blow on it gently and watch it spin. Then blow harder.

workedExamples.title: 1 - Following the Energy of a Falling Mango
workedExamples.prompt: A ripe mango hangs high in a tree. Suddenly the stalk breaks and the mango falls to the ground with a thud. Let us describe the energy changes.
workedExamples.solution:
Start: While the mango is high up and still, it has stored gravitational potential energy because of its height.

Falling: As it falls, its height gets smaller, so the potential energy changes into kinetic energy. The mango moves faster and faster.

The thud: When it hits the ground, the kinetic energy is transferred to the ground and the air, turning into a little sound energy (the thud) and a tiny bit of heat energy.

Conclusion: No energy was lost. It simply changed form, from potential to kinetic to sound and heat.

workedExamples.title: 2 - Comparing Kinetic Energy
workedExamples.prompt: Two friends roll balls across the sand. Amina rolls her ball slowly. Farah rolls a ball of the same size much faster. Which ball has more kinetic energy?
workedExamples.solution:
Remember the rule: The faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

Compare: Both balls are the same size, so weight is not the difference. The only difference is speed.

Answer: Farah's faster ball has more kinetic energy. That is why it would roll further and be harder to stop.

Worked Example 3 — The Solar Lamp

workedExamples.title: 3 - The Solar Lamp
workedExamples.prompt: Khadija has a small solar lamp. During the day she leaves it in the sunshine, and at night it glows so she can study. Describe the energy journey.
workedExamples.solution:
Daytime: Light energy from the Sun hits the solar panel on the lamp.

Storing: The panel changes the light energy into electrical energy, which is stored in the lamp's small battery as chemical energy.

Night-time: When Khadija switches it on, the stored energy changes back into electrical energy and then into light energy so she can see.

Conclusion: The Sun's free energy was collected, stored, and used later. This is renewable energy at work.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Energy is best described as: (a) a kind of food (b) the ability to do work or cause change (c) a type of metal (d) a colour
workedExamples.solution: (b) the ability to do work or cause change. This is the scientific meaning of energy.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which type of energy does a running goat have? (a) light energy (b) sound energy (c) kinetic energy (d) chemical energy
workedExamples.solution: (c) kinetic energy. Anything that moves, like a running goat, has kinetic (movement) energy.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: What type of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band? (a) elastic potential energy (b) light energy (c) sound energy (d) thermal energy
workedExamples.solution: (a) elastic potential energy. Stretching stores energy that is released when you let go.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: The greatest source of energy for the Earth is: (a) charcoal (b) the Sun (c) batteries (d) wind
workedExamples.solution: (b) the Sun. Almost all energy on Earth begins with the Sun, including food and wind.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a renewable energy source? (a) oil (b) coal (c) solar energy (d) petrol
workedExamples.solution: (c) solar energy. The Sun will not run out, so solar energy is renewable. Oil, coal and petrol are non-renewable.

activities.title: The Swinging Pendulum (Kinetic and Potential Energy)
activities.materials: A piece of string or strong thread, about 50 cm long; A small heavy object such as a metal washer, a bunch of keys, or a small stone in a cloth bag; A fixed point to hang it from, such as a door handle, a hook, or the back of a chair
steps: Tie the heavy object firmly to one end of the string.
Tie or hold the other end of the string to a fixed point so the object can swing freely.
Pull the object gently to one side so it is raised up, and hold it still. Notice that it is now higher up.
Let go (do not push) and watch the object swing back and forth.
Watch closely: at which point does it move fastest? At which points does it pause?

activities.title: The Sunshine Water Warmer (Light and Heat Energy)
activities.materials: Two identical cups or small jars; The same amount of water in each cup (fill them equally); A piece of dark cloth or dark paper, and a piece of white or light cloth or paper; A sunny spot outdoors or by a window; Optional: a thermometer if you have one, or just use your finger to feel
steps: Fill both cups with the same amount of water at the same temperature.
Wrap one cup in dark cloth and the other in white cloth.
If you have a thermometer, measure and write down the starting temperature of each cup.
Place both cups side by side in a sunny spot.
Wait for about one hour. Try to keep everything else the same, so it is a fair test.

activities.title: The Rubber Band Launcher (Elastic Potential Energy)
activities.materials: A rubber band; A small light object to launch, such as a scrunched-up ball of paper; A measuring tape, a ruler, or a length of string you can mark; A clear, open floor space with nothing breakable nearby
steps: Hook the rubber band over your thumb, and place the paper ball in the band like a little sling.
Pull the band back only a small amount (for example, 5 cm) and let go, aiming at the open floor, never at anyone.
Measure how far the paper ball travelled and write it down.
Now pull the band back further (for example, 10 cm) and launch again. Measure the distance.
Try a third, even bigger stretch. Measure again.

activities.title: The Pinwheel and the Wind (Kinetic Energy of Air)
activities.materials: A square of paper (about 15 cm by 15 cm); A pin, a thumbtack, or a thin stick to hold the centre; A pencil with an eraser, a straw, or a stick to act as the handle; Scissors (ask an adult to help with cutting)
steps: Fold the paper square corner to corner both ways to find the centre, then unfold it.
Carefully cut along each fold from the corner towards the centre, but stop before you reach the middle.
Bring every other corner into the centre to form the pinwheel shape, and pin them at the middle.
Pin the pinwheel loosely onto the handle so it can spin freely.
Blow on it gently and watch it spin. Then blow harder.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: Observe: The Great Rule: Energy Cannot Be Created or Destroyed
activities.materials: A piece of string or strong thread, about 50 cm long; A small heavy object such as a metal washer, a bunch of keys, or a small stone in a cloth bag; A fixed point to hang it from, such as a door handle, a hook, or the back of a chair
steps: Look for an example of the great rule: energy cannot be created or destroyed around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Energy and Kinetic energy.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: What Energy Is
rules.text: Energy is the ability to do work or to make a change happen. You cannot always see energy, but you can always see what it does. Everything that moves, heats up, glows, or makes a sound is using energy.

rules.title: Energy Is Never Lost
rules.text: Energy is never truly lost. It only changes form or moves to a new place. When something slows down or cools down, its energy has spread out, often as heat. No machine can make energy from nothing. This is a rule that nature never breaks.

rules.title: Speed and Kinetic Energy
rules.text: Remember the rule: The faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

rules.title: Energy: The Big Picture
rules.text: You have learned that energy is the ability to make things happen. It comes in many forms, it moves and changes, but it is never created or destroyed. The Sun is the great giver of energy, and caring for energy helps us care for the Earth.

terms: The ability to do work or cause a change.
The energy of a moving object.
Stored energy ready to be used.
Energy that lets us see and travels from bright things.
Energy of vibrations that we hear.
Energy moving from one object to another.
Energy changing from one form to another.
A force that slows moving things and makes heat.
Energy that will not run out.

vocabulary.meaning: Stored energy ready to be used.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy that lets us see and travels from bright things.
vocabulary.example: Light energy is the form of energy that lets you see the world.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy of vibrations that we hear.
vocabulary.example: When you hear the call to prayer travel across the town, you are hearing sound energy.
Electrical energy is the energy that flows through wires to power the machines and devices we use.
The place that energy comes from is called an energy source.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy moving from one object to another.
vocabulary.example: When energy moves from one object to another, we call it an energy transfer.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy changing from one form to another.
vocabulary.example: When energy changes from one form into a different form, we call it an energy transformation.

vocabulary.meaning: A force that slows moving things and makes heat.
vocabulary.example: The rubbing that slows things down is caused by a force called friction.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy that will not run out.
vocabulary.example: Explain the difference between renewable energy (like solar and wind) and non-renewable energy (like oil and charcoal).

commonMistakes: Thinking energy disappears when things stop.
It looks like it vanishes, but energy is never destroyed.
Thinking only moving things have energy.
Still things can hold stored (potential) energy too.
Thinking heavy always means more energy.
Speed matters too, not just weight.
Wall electricity is high-voltage and dangerous.
Believing a machine can make free energy.

connections.text: Electrical energy, circuits, and batteries build directly on this unit.
Light and sound are both forms of energy you will study more deeply.
Food gives living things chemical energy; the Sun powers plants through photosynthesis.
The Sun drives weather, wind, and the seasons with its energy.
Solar and wind energy are important for communities across East Africa.
Measuring, recording, and comparing energy data uses counting and simple graphs.

realProblems.answer: Solar panels make electricity from sunlight without needing a power station or wires from far away. Since East Africa is very sunny, Halima's family could light their home and charge devices using free, clean, renewable energy right where they live.

realProblems.prompt: Omar boils water from the well before drinking it. What form of energy makes the water safe, and where does that energy come from if he uses a charcoal stove?
realProblems.answer: Heat (thermal) energy makes the water safe by killing germs. If Omar uses a charcoal stove, that heat energy comes from the chemical energy stored in the charcoal, which is released when it burns.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Energy, Kinetic energy, Potential energy — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Heat (thermal) energy makes the water safe by killing germs. If Omar uses a charcoal stove, that heat energy comes from the chemical energy stored in the charcoal, which is released when it burns.

realProblems.prompt: The coast near Berbera is very windy. Explain how this wind could be used to make electricity.
realProblems.answer: The wind carries kinetic energy. If it pushes the blades of a wind turbine, the turbine spins and changes the wind's movement energy into electrical energy for homes.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Energy, Kinetic energy, Potential energy — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: The wind carries kinetic energy. If it pushes the blades of a wind turbine, the turbine spins and changes the wind's movement energy into electrical energy for homes.

realProblems.prompt: Aisha eats a good breakfast of canjeero and dates before school. Explain how this food gives her energy to learn and play.
realProblems.answer: The canjeero and dates contain chemical potential energy. Aisha's body unlocks this stored energy and uses it to power her muscles and brain, giving her the energy to learn and play.

realProblems.prompt: During the day, the sun is bright. Explain why using daylight instead of switching on lamps helps save energy.
realProblems.answer: Daylight is free energy from the Sun. Using it instead of lamps means no electricity or fuel is used, so energy and money are saved and nothing is wasted.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Energy, Kinetic energy, Potential energy — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Daylight is free energy from the Sun. Using it instead of lamps means no electricity or fuel is used, so energy and money are saved and nothing is wasted.

realProblems.prompt: A man claims he has built a machine that runs forever and makes more energy than it uses. Using the great rule of energy, explain why this is impossible.
realProblems.answer: It is impossible because energy cannot be created from nothing. A machine can only pass along the energy it is given, and some of that energy always leaks away as heat because of friction. So no machine can ever give out more energy than it takes in.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, explain what energy is.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Energy is the ability to do work or to make something change or happen. Accept any answer with this meaning.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the six main forms of energy you have learned.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The six main forms are: light, heat (thermal), sound, movement (kinetic), stored (potential), and electrical energy.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one local example of heat energy and one local example of light energy.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Heat energy example: a charcoal stove, the Sun's warmth, or hot tea. Light energy example: sunlight, a torch, a lamp, or a lamp flame. Accept any correct local example.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy? Give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Renewable energy will not run out (example: solar or wind). Non-renewable energy will run out one day (example: oil, coal, or natural gas).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what happens to the energy when you kick a football and it rolls to a stop.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Your foot transfers kinetic energy to the ball, so it moves. As it rolls, friction turns the movement energy into a little heat and sound, which spread out, so the ball slows and stops. The energy is not lost, only changed.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is the Sun called the great source of energy for almost everything?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because the Sun gives light and heat directly, and it is also the starting point for wind, for the growth of plants, and therefore for food. Most energy on Earth can be traced back to the Sun.

rounds.prompt: What form of energy do we hear with our ears?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: sound energy. We hear sound energy, which travels as vibrations through the air.

rounds.prompt: Why does a rolling ball slow down and stop?
choices: energy turns into heat and sound and spreads out
rounds.answer: energy turns into heat and sound and spreads out
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: its movement energy turns into heat and sound and spreads out. The energy is not destroyed, only scattered.

rounds.prompt: Which type of energy does a running goat have?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: kinetic energy. Anything that moves, like a running goat, has kinetic (movement) energy.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a renewable energy source?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: solar energy. The Sun will not run out, so solar energy is renewable. Oil, coal and petrol are non-renewable.

games.title: Real-Life Round: Energy transfer
games.description: Practise energy transfer through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A solar panel changes light energy into:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: electrical energy. A solar panel turns the Sun's light energy into electricity.

rounds.prompt: Which of these carries kinetic energy?
choices: a still rock on the ground
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the wind on the coast. Moving air has kinetic energy; the still and switched-off things do not.

rounds.prompt: What type of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: elastic potential energy. Stretching stores energy that is released when you let go.

rounds.prompt: When a mango falls from a tree, its potential energy changes into:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: kinetic energy. As the mango falls, its stored (potential) energy becomes movement (kinetic) energy.

games.title: Spot the Error: Energy transformation
games.description: Practise energy transformation through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which food gives your body energy?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: dates and bariis. Food holds chemical energy that our bodies use.

rounds.prompt: Energy is best described as:
choices: the ability to do work or cause change
rounds.answer: the ability to do work or cause change
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the ability to do work or cause change. This is the scientific meaning of energy.

rounds.prompt: The greatest source of energy for the Earth is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the Sun. Almost all energy on Earth begins with the Sun, including food and wind.

rounds.prompt: Energy can be:
choices: changed from one form to another
rounds.answer: changed from one form to another
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: changed from one form to another. Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed or moved.

selfAssessment: I can explain what energy is and why it is needed for anything to happen.
I can name and describe the main forms of energy: light, heat, sound, movement (kinetic), stored (potential), and electrical energy.
I can identify different energy sources, such as the Sun, food, wind, moving water, charcoal, and fuel.
I can describe how energy is transferred from one object to another and how it changes from one form to another.
I can state the big rule of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed or moved.
I can explain the difference between renewable energy (like solar and wind) and non-renewable energy (like oil and charcoal).
I can give practical examples of how to save energy in your own home and community.
I can investigate energy questions fairly and record what you observe.
